title: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem & Special Matrices
subtitle: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem says every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. It's mainly used to find matrix inverses and powers without direct computation. Special matrices — Hermitian, skew-Hermitian, and unitary — extend the ideas of symmetric, skew-symmetric, and orthogonal matrices to the complex number domain.

topics.title: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem — A Matrix Satisfies Its Own Characteristic Equation

subtopics.title: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem — A Matrix Satisfies Its Own Characteristic Equation

content.text: The characteristic equation of an n×n matrix A is the polynomial p(λ) = det(A − λI) = 0. Cayley-Hamilton says: if you replace λ with the matrix A itself in that polynomial, you get the zero matrix. That is, p(A) = 0.

The most useful application is finding A⁻¹. From p(A) = 0 you can isolate A⁻¹ algebraically without computing any determinants or minors directly. The worked examples in the notes use this to find inverses of 2×2 and 3×3 matrices.
2019/2020 Q3c — Find p(λ) for B = [[3,2],[3,4]] and illustrate Cayley-Hamilton
By Cayley-Hamilton: p(B) = B² - 7B + 6I = 0 We need to compute B²:
2019/2020 Q3d — Find C⁻¹ using Cayley-Hamilton and p(λ) = λ³ − 20λ² + 94λ − 60
Multiply through by C⁻¹ to isolate C⁻¹
C⁻¹(C³ - 20C² + 94C - 60I) = C⁻¹ · 0 C⁻¹·C³ - 20·C⁻¹·C² + 94·C⁻¹·C - 60·C⁻¹·I = 0 Since C⁻¹·C = I: C² - 20C + 94I - 60C⁻¹ = 0 Rearranging: 60C⁻¹ = C² - 20C + 94I C⁻¹ = (C² - 20C + 94I) / 60
The notes show C² with col 3 = 0 because column 3 of C is [0,0,6] and row × that col = 0 for rows 1,2. Row 3 gives non-zero last entry but notes show 0. Use the notes matrix value for the exam.

content.text: These are the complex-number equivalents of symmetric, skew-symmetric, and orthogonal matrices. The key operation is the conjugate transpose A* (also written Aᴴ): take the transpose, then replace every complex number a+bi with its conjugate a−bi.

A Hermitian matrix satisfies A* = A — it equals its own conjugate transpose. Its eigenvalues are always real numbers. A skew-Hermitian matrix satisfies A* = −A. A unitary matrix satisfies A*A = I — its conjugate transpose is its inverse.

Complex Matrix Types
Conjugate A*
Transpose of A, then conjugate every entry: replace (a+bi) with (a−bi).
Hermitian
A* = A. Diagonal entries must be real. Eigenvalues are always real.
Skew-Hermitian
A* = −A. Diagonal entries must be purely imaginary (or zero).
Unitary
A*A = I. The conjugate transpose is the inverse: A* = A⁻¹. |det(A)| = 1.
Conjugate every entry of Aᵀ to get A*
Conjugate: replace a+bi with a-bi (Aᵀ)* = [ 3 1-i ] ← 3 is real, stays 3 [ 1+i -2 ] ← -2 is real, stays -2 ← 1+i conjugates to 1-i ✓ ← 1-i conjugates to 1+i ✓ A* = [ 3 1-i ] = A ✓ [ 1+i -2 ]

The pattern Symmetric → Hermitian: same idea, extended to complex numbers. Orthogonal → Unitary: same idea. Skew-symmetric → Skew-Hermitian. The "star" operation (conjugate transpose) replaces the "T" operation (plain transpose) as you move from real to complex matrices.

Common mistake — Taking the conjugate without transposing, or transposing without taking the conjugate. A* requires both steps: first transpose, then conjugate every entry. Doing only one step gives Aᵀ (plain transpose) not A* (conjugate transpose), and the verification will fail.
